simple: a machine that notices the world, decides what to do, and then moves or changes something, again and again.
analogy: a body with senses, a brain and muscles.
precise: a machine that measures its surroundings with sensors, computes a decision with a program, and acts on the world with actuators, in a repeating loop.
source: D2 §1 of F9-01, D1 §1.3 of F9-01 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: the three jobs a robot does over and over: notice, decide, do.
analogy: Amara noticing the bend, deciding to steer, and steering.
precise: a way to describe a robot's work as a repeating cycle of measuring (sense), computing a decision (think) and commanding its actuators (act). Control engineers call this "the basic feedback loop of sensing, computation, and actuation".
source: D1 §1.3 of F9-01 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a part that lets a robot notice something, like light or distance.
analogy: your eyes, ears and skin.
precise: a device that measures a physical quantity and turns it into a signal or number the robot's computer can read.
source: D2 §1 of F9-01, D1 §1.3 of F9-01 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a part that makes the robot move or change something.
analogy: your muscles.
precise: a device that turns a command from the computer into motion or another physical effect; an electric motor is one example.
source: D2 §1 of F9-01 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a program that pretends to be the robot and its world, so you can test safely.
analogy: practising bicycle balance on a game screen before the real park.
precise: software that computes how a model of a robot and its surroundings would behave, step by step, so programs can be tested without real hardware. In this course, the simulators are tiny C++ programs written by this university; they are the course's own teaching tools and stand in for a full 3D robotics simulator such as Gazebo, which later courses use.
source: R1 of F9-01, D14 of F9-01 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: the number a sensor gives when the robot asks it "what do you notice now?"
analogy: how bright the line looks to Ravi at one moment.
precise: one measurement value produced by a sensor at one moment, in the sensor's own units.
source: D3 §2 of F9-02, D10 §2.1.1.4 of F9-02 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a sensor that tells how bright something is.
analogy: your eyes telling light from dark.
precise: a sensor whose output changes with the amount of light reaching it; a reflective sensor pairs its light detector with a small light source (in the example datasheet an infrared one, which people cannot see) and reports how much light the surface below reflects.
source: D11 Description of F9-02 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a sensor that tells how far away the nearest thing in front is.
analogy: judging with your eyes how far the wall is.
precise: a range sensor; some send out a pulse of sound or light and time the echo that comes back from an object.
source: D12 §1.1 of F9-02, D13 §3.6.2 of F9-02 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a sensor that only says "I touched something" or "I did not".
analogy: the skin on your hand feeling a wall.
precise: in this course, a contact switch that closes (or opens) when pressed; its reading has only two values.
source: F9-02 chapter definition (no external source needed)

simple: small random wobbles in a sensor's readings.
analogy: the line looking slightly different every time a cloud moves.
precise: the part of a measurement that differs from the true value in ways that change from reading to reading; even very precise instruments have some.
source: D10 §2.1.1.4 of F9-02, D3 §1 of F9-02 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a dividing number: below it means one thing, above it means another.
analogy: "if the yard looks this dark or darker, I am on the line".
precise: a fixed value a program compares a reading with to turn it into a yes/no decision.
source: F9-02 chapter definition (no external source needed)

simple: to measure known things first, so you can set your numbers well.
analogy: looking at the white line and the grey yard before the race starts.
precise: to determine how a sensor's readings relate to known conditions (here: readings on floor and on line) and set the program's constants from those measurements.
source: D10 §2.3.1 of F9-02 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a part that turns electricity into turning.
analogy: a muscle that pulls when your brain tells it to.
precise: an electric motor is an actuator that turns electrical power into rotation of its shaft; a robot's program controls it indirectly, through a motor driver that switches the power.
source: D2 §1 of F9-03, D8 §15.1.6 of F9-03 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: the instruction the program gives a motor, such as "turn this fast".
analogy: your brain telling a leg how hard to push the pedal.
precise: the value a control program sends to a motor driver; what the wheel then really does can differ from it, for example when a wheel slips, so robots measure the result.
source: D2 §13.4 of F9-03 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a sensor that counts how much a wheel has turned.
analogy: counting the turns of a wheel.
precise: a sensor on a motor or wheel shaft that measures how far the shaft has turned, as counts; distance travelled is estimated from the counts and the wheel size.
source: D2 §1 of F9-03, D2 §13.4 of F9-03 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: steering by turning two side wheels at different speeds.
analogy: Kofi and Ines pushing the two cart wheels.
precise: a wheeled robot with two independently driven wheels on one axle; equal wheel speeds drive straight, different speeds turn it toward the slower wheel's side.
source: D2 §13.1 of F9-03, D9 Differential drive of F9-03 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: exact steps that a computer follows, one after another.
analogy: Sione's plan for the ride.
precise: a sequence of instructions that a computer executes exactly as written; a robot's program turns sensor readings into motor commands.
source: D5 §5.1.1 of F9-04, D5 §5.1.4 of F9-04 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a part of a program that repeats.
analogy: look, pedal, look, pedal.
precise: a control structure that executes its body repeatedly; a while loop in C++ repeats as long as its condition is true.
source: D6 §8.6.2 of F9-04, R1 of F9-04 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a question with the answer yes or no.
analogy: "Is that the blue gate?"
precise: an expression that evaluates to true or false and decides whether an if branch runs or a loop goes round again.
source: D6 §8.5.2 of F9-04, D6 §8.6.2 of F9-04 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a rule that stops the robot after too many rounds, even if the job is not done.
analogy: "I have gone much too far, I will stop and call home."
precise: a maximum number of loop iterations (or a maximum time) after which the program stops on purpose, so that a wrong rule cannot make the robot run forever.
source: R2 of F9-04 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: the lines a program prints about what it did, one after another.
analogy: a diary of the ride.
precise: a time-ordered record of a program's actions and values, used to understand and debug its behaviour.
source: R1 of F9-04 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a loop that keeps checking how far you are from what you want, and corrects a bit each time.
analogy: riding a bicycle and correcting your balance.
precise: a feedback loop that repeatedly measures a system's output, compares it with a target, and computes a command that reduces the difference.
source: D1 §1.3 of F9-05 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: using what you just measured to decide your next action.
analogy: seeing that you drifted, and steering because of it.
precise: the use of a measured output of a system to influence its input; a loop with feedback is called closed loop, one without is open loop (taught in F9-16).
source: D1 §1.1 of F9-05 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: where you want to be.
analogy: right on the chalk line.
precise: the desired value of the controlled quantity; here, a distance from the line of zero. Engineers call it the reference or the setpoint.
source: D1 §11.1 of F9-05 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: how far you are from where you want to be.
analogy: how far Lucía's wheel is from the chalk.
precise: the difference between the measured value and the target; in this chapter, the measured distance from the line (target zero), positive to the right and negative to the left. Control books usually subtract the other way round (error = target − measured) and then use a plus sign in the rule; both describe the same correction. Not the same as a program "error" or bug (F0-08).
source: D1 §1.6 of F9-05, D1 §11.1 of F9-05 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a number that says how strongly to correct.
analogy: how hard Lucía turns the handlebars for each bit she is off.
precise: the constant that multiplies the error to produce the correction; with this chapter's error, the proportional rule is correction = − gain × error.
source: D1 §11.1 of F9-05 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a little off, steer a little; far off, steer a lot.
analogy: Arjun's advice, "gently".
precise: a control law in which the command is proportional to the error; it is the P of PID, taught fully in F9-17.
source: D1 §1.6 of F9-05, D1 §11.1 of F9-05 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: correcting so hard that you shoot past the target to the other side.
analogy: Lucía yanking the handlebars and zig-zagging.
precise: a response that crosses the target (overshoot) because the correction is too large for the system; with this chapter's rule it happens when the gain is larger than 1.
source: R3 of F9-05 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a robot that drives along a line on the floor.
analogy: Lucía riding along the chalk.
precise: in this course, a mobile robot that uses one or more floor sensors (reflective light sensors, F9-02) to measure its position relative to a line and steers to stay on it.
source: D11 Applications of F9-05 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a pretend world made of squares, like a board game.
analogy: Mei's paper map with streets.
precise: a simulated environment divided into cells; each cell is free or blocked, and the robot moves from cell to cell. Robot mapping uses the same idea: an occupancy grid, whose cells are occupied or free.
source: D3 §3 of F9-06, R1 of F9-06 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: one instruction for the robot, like "go forward one square".
analogy: "turn right at the bakery".
precise: in this chapter's simulator, one character: F moves forward one cell, L turns 90 degrees left, R turns 90 degrees right, on the spot.
source: R1 of F9-06 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: the direction the robot is facing.
analogy: which way your bicycle's front wheel points.
precise: the robot's orientation; in the grid world one of east, south, west or north. "Left" and "right" are measured from the robot's own heading, not from the map. A wheeled robot's heading angle is one of the numbers that describe where it is.
source: D2 §13.3.1 of F9-06 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: trying the program to see if it does what you wanted.
analogy: tracing the route on the map with your finger.
precise: an execution of a program with known inputs whose output is compared with the expected result.
source: R1 of F9-06 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a big, easy button or switch that makes the robot stop at once.
analogy: the brakes on your bicycle.
precise: a stop control that removes the power to the robot's motors (or otherwise forces them to stop) immediately and stays active until a person deliberately resets it; in this university it must be a physical switch that does not rely on the robot's program.
source: S1 of F9-07 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: once switched on, it stays on until someone switches it off on purpose.
analogy: a door that locks when it shuts, and needs a key to open.
precise: a state that, once set by an event, remains set after the event ends, until an explicit reset.
source: R1 of F9-07 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: the fastest the robot is allowed to go, whatever its program asks for.
analogy: riding slowly near the playground.
precise: an upper bound applied to every motor command before it is sent, so that no part of the program can command a faster speed.
source: R1 of F9-07, S1 of F9-07 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: an empty space around the robot that people stay out of while it can move.
analogy: the path being clear before you ride fast.
precise: a marked area around a robot that is kept free of people, animals and objects whenever the robot is powered and able to move.
source: S1 of F9-07 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)

simple: a grown-up who watches, helps and can stop everything.
analogy: Amara's uncle walking next to her bicycle.
precise: the continuous presence of a responsible adult who has read the kit's instructions and controls the emergency stop during a real-robot activity.
source: S1 of F9-07 (checked in the verification pass 2026-10-10)
